summary: We turned NASA–ISRO NISAR L2 pixel-offset (GOFF) data into a validated ice-speed map of Sermeq Kujalleq (Jakobshavn Isbræ), one of Greenland’s fastest and largest outlet glaciers, using a 12-day pair from 15 to 27 December 2025. We documented a step-by-step, open-source QGIS workflow that filters noise, corrects the radar’s systematic offset using bedrock, and converts offsets into m/day. Compared with an independent Sentinel-1 product, our map agrees to within a few hundredths of a metre per day (bias −0.07 m/day) over about 24,000 km². Greenland’s ice loss is a major driver of sea-level rise, and NISAR is new, so scientists need transparent, reproducible and quality-checked ways to use its data.
details:
Our product is a reproducible workflow plus a velocity map. How it works:

  1. We use the NISAR GOFF product (track 170, frame 053; reference 15 Dec 2025, secondary 27 Dec 2025, Δt = 12 days), which gives along-track and slant-range displacement in metres for three window sizes (layers 1–3), together with an SNR layer.
  2. We keep only pixels with SNR > 20, a threshold chosen from the noise floor over open sea (99th percentile of SNR ≈ 19).
  3. We measure the systematic offset over bedrock (which should not move) at two sites and subtract it. The north–south difference was about 4 m and was found in all three layers, which shows it is a real instrument/ionosphere effect rather than random noise.
  4. We convert to speed: v = √[(az − b_az)² + ((rg − b_rg)/sin θ)²] / Δt, with θ ≈ 40° (an approximation).
  5. We merge the three layers (layer 3 has the lowest noise, so it has priority where valid), apply an ice mask and remove isolated pixels (sieve).
  6. We validate against NSIDC-0766 (Sentinel-1, 16–27 Dec 2025) on a common 200 m grid using the median.

Technology: QGIS 4.2.2, GDAL 3.13.3, GeoTIFF, spreadsheet statistics.

Results: over 607,176 pixels (about 24,300 km²) where our speed is below 11 m/day, bias is −0.067 m/day and RMSE is about 0.257 m/day. Layers 1, 2 and 3 agree within 3–5% wherever all three are valid. Residual speed over bedrock is about 0.14–0.19 m/day, so we advise trusting speeds above roughly 0.5 m/day.

Limitations: at the fastest part near the calving front, speeds above about 11–13 m/day are reported as lower bounds, because the offset search window probably limits measurable displacement (suspected, not confirmed), and layer 3 has no data there. The bedrock correction is a constant, and the incidence angle is approximate.

Goal and benefits: to give students and researchers a transparent starting point for using NISAR offsets on glaciers, showing both what works and where the data stop being reliable.

Use of AI
We used Claude (Anthropic) to explain the NISAR GOFF product and glacier concepts, plan the processing workflow, write QGIS formulas and step-by-step instructions, interpret screenshots of our intermediate results, run preliminary checks on our exported layer-1 GeoTIFFs (value statistics and noise floor), and draft this submission and our documentation. All data processing on our own files was run by the team in QGIS, and we checked the results ourselves against the independent reference.
